newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy left leader warns of coalition instability.
newsitem.headline: Italy left leader warns of coalition instability.

text.p: The leader of the largest party in Italy's coalition said stability would suffer if the governing centre-left failed to promote lasting constitutional reform, a leading newspaper reported on Friday.

Massimo D'Alema made his comments to Rome's daily La Repubblica as media reported a chill in relations between Prime Minister Romano Prodi and D'Alema's ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) over how to deal with the opposition.

"After last April's success (in national elections), we said clearly that that was not the end of the transition in Italy but that the centre-left had the duty to guarantee a decisive push towards constitutional reform," D'Alema said.
"Today, in the most explicit terms possible, we say that if the centre-left is not able to promote a process of reform, the stability of the government will suffer...," he added.
"Reforms are necessary and they can't be put off," he said.
D'Alema is leading negotiations to set up a cross-party parliamentary commission to work out a much needed reform of Italy electoral and parliamentary system.

However, parties within Prodi's coalition are divided over what kind of reform is needed, while the opposition centre-right led by former prime minister silvio Berlusconi wants assurances before joining any commission.

The hardleft Communist Refoundation, which guarantees the Prodi government's majority in the lower house, has threatened to withdraw its support if the PDS sides with the centre-right over the reform issue.
Most newspapers on Friday ran headlines about what they said was a chilling in relations between D'Alema and Prodi over the prime minister's treatment of the opposition.
"D'Alema-Prodi, it's Cold War," ran a headline in Turin's La Stampa.
La Stampa said Prodi and D'Alema had become engaged in a "dialogue of the deaf" which is raising tensions between the premier and the largest party in his six-month-old coalition to alarm levels.
PDS leaders said after a meeting of the party's executive on Thursday that Prodi should take a softer line with the opposition and seek a modus vivendi that promotes dialogue.

Some PDS leaders have accused Prodi of using terms considered too harsh, such as saying that the centre-right wanted to sabotage the government and asserting that Berlusconi was not "culturally" fit to head an eventual reform commission.
The Corriere Della Sera newspaper of Milan likened the recent tensions between D'Alema and Prodi to those of a separated couple forced to live under the same roof.
Despite his own differences with the opposition, D'Alema has been trying to keep a dialogue open with Berlusconi and the centre-right over reforms.

D'Alema and Berlusconi agreed at a meeting on Tuesday that talks over the planned commission should be put off until parliament finishes examining the 1997 budget. The financial bill has to be passed into law by the end of the year.
The right wants to introduce a presidential-style government and hardright leader Gianfranco Fini has demanded a guarantee that the proposed commission will move in this direction.
Refoundation and other government supporters, including the centrist Popular Party, are opposed to such an electoral system.
Politicians have talked for 15 years about the need to modernise Italy's 1948 constitution and end the history of revolving-door governments.
Commentators believe that the huge corruption scandals at the start of the 1990s, which destroyed the old ruling elite, would usher in swift reform, but this has not happened.
